Biological Memories Beyond the Brain

Biological memories beyond the brain — immune “trained immunity” and epigenetic cell memory show durable, experience-dependent changes outside neural tissue.

Biological memory extends beyond neurons. Two paradigmatic cases are immune trained immunity—long‑lasting, experience‑dependent tuning of innate immune cells—and epigenetic cell memory—stable gene‑regulatory states that persist through cell divisions and sometimes across generations. Both involve lasting reprogramming that modifies future responses to stimuli.

Immune “Trained Immunity”

  • Innate cells (monocytes, macrophages, NK cells) show memory‑like enhanced responses after a primary exposure, independent of T/B cell receptors.
  • Mechanisms: chromatin remodeling (e.g., H3K4me3, H3K27ac), altered metabolism (glycolysis, mevalonate), and persistent transcriptional programs.
  • Human evidence: BCG vaccination induces genome‑wide epigenetic and functional reprogramming and protects against heterologous challenges.
  • Proof‑of‑principle in absence of adaptive immunity: monocyte‑dependent protection in lymphocyte‑deficient mice after Candida exposure.

Epigenetic Cell Memory

  • Stable gene expression states via DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin architecture, and small RNAs can encode past exposures.
  • These states can persist through mitosis and, in certain taxa and contexts, across generations.
  • Plants provide clear models of stress memory (heat, drought, cold) with documented regulatory marks and phenotypic carry‑over.

Cross‑Domain Pattern

Across neural, immune, and somatic systems, the shared pattern is:

experience → durable molecular reprogramming → altered future response

This reframes “memory” as a general biological principle of persistence with plasticity, relevant to infection susceptibility, autoimmunity, cancer immunotherapy, adaptation to stress, ageing trajectories, and even ecological resilience.
